item.title: What's the Meat of the Matter?
item.description:
🏛️ Independent Policy & Society • The India Forum

Author: Sayan Deori, Tanya Chaudhary, Shobhit Mahajan, Rahul Goel, Sudha Narayanan, Shree Saha, Aditi Gautam, Thomas Reardon, S. Gunasekaran, Seema Mundoli, Somdatta Karak, Salik Ahmad

Food is extremely political in India, embroiled in the larger politics of religion and caste. Over the last decade, these controversies have been further heightened. Basic nutritional food like eggs for children in schools has been scrapped in several states. Eating one’s favourite mutton curry during Hindu festivals may not be possible as the state shuts down meat shops during that period. Public spaces are segregated based on diet preferences, like when a mess in IIT Bombay introduced 'pure veg’ dining table. Vigilante mobs have raided kitchens and fridges on suspicion of beef consumption, and state diplomatic banquets have turned into ‘pure vegetarian’ galas. These are not isolated incidents, but connected events engineered and enabled by the current majoritarian Hindutva regime.

Karpagam highlights the caste angle of vegetarian food in India, and how the vegetarian imposition is carried out in India by the state...

The Meat of the Matter: How the Politics of Food Shapes Our Health by Sylvia Karpagam sits at the intersection of nutrition science and the politics of meat and animal source foods that is being played out in contemporary India. She enters the debate on the political and nutritional economy of food and the politics of idolising normative diets. Karpagam is a medical doctor and has faced online trolling for her views on food and nutrition, something she mentions in the book as well—these include casteist slurs like ‘rice bag convert’. Her book picks up questions related to food politics in contemporary India, and elaborates on them through a synthesis of evidence and data from published studies related to nutrition and public health.

The narrative thread of the book is the fictitious story of Princess Amudam of Arogya Nadu, a prosperous kingdom high on the Human Development Index, journeying to Starva Pradesh, a kingdom performing poorly on every variable of human development and public health. Along the princess’s passage between the kingdoms, Karapagam weaves in her account of contemporary Indian malnutrition and food issues. This story is threaded into all the chapters. The book can be broadly categorised into three categories for the readers: human nutrition, the burden of malnutrition, and the vegetarian and meat discourse that shapes policies.

The first three chapters provide a clinical register of human nutrition from the role of various macro- and micro-nutrients like proteins, fats, minerals and vitamins. They are textbook styled, outlining the scientific understanding of nutrients, their sources, and their bodily benefits, through fact-boxes of facts and blobs of information in sections like “Did You Know?” and “Debunking Myths on the Plate”. The end of each chapter has bulleted “Key Takeaways”. While it felt slightly stretchy at parts, the synthesis of nutritional science over many decades builds a coherent narrative on nutrition.

From nutrition science, Karpagam moves onto malnutrition, drawing on population level data and studies across time periods and regions. She illustrates the high burden of undernutrition in India and its indicators like stunting, wasting, and underweight, through the National Family Health Surveys (NFHS) and the Comprehensive National Nutrition Survey (CNNS 2019). She also discusses the high prevalence of nutritional anaemia, mostly caused due to iron deficiency, to which women of reproductive age groups are the most vulnerable. Through these chapters, Karpagam also busts fads popular on social media, including 'Soya is Super Food', and  'Millets are Magical', through a careful explanation of nutrition bioavailability—how much of the theoretical nutrition of the food item the body can actually absorb—and dietary guidelines.

The third engagement of the book is with the politics of food and its manifestation in everyday life. Karpagam highlights the caste angle of vegetarian food in India, and how the vegetarian imposition is carried out in India by the state through ideological interference in public nutritional programmes. She highlights how concerns over ‘purity’ have caused eggs to be removed from midday meals in schools in several states.

In particular, she critiques the Akshya Patra Foundation (APF), whose collaboration with state governments in supplying school lunches promotes ‘sattvic food’. She mentions that “the foundation has a religious prerogative of advocating a de facto vegeterian diet, strictly avoiding meat, fish and eggs, and considers onions and garlic in food as lower modes of nature which inhibits spiritual advancement”. Not only this, but she also flags the APF’s financial opacity and its strong caste linkages and state patronages that it receives. These kinds of organisations are complicit in advancing and making a Hindutva state.

Karpagam challenges the narrative of the vegetarian discourse of nutrition by juxtaposing it with majoritarianism.

Karpagam also sheds light on the EAT-Lancet 2019 report and the “sustainable diet for planetary health” agenda that was being circulated and also platformed and promoted by India's food safety regulator. She touches upon the big food corporate nexus in nutrition policies. The EAT Lancet report 2019 propagated a global narrative to shift from a meat-based diet to a plant-based diet, and particularly idolised India as an ideal vegetarian society. She criticises the report's prescriptions: a clamp down on animal source foods, equating them as being as unhealthy as sugar, a hint at moving towards a plant based diet, and looking for “alternative proteins”. She mentions big corporations are privy to this and have appropriated the term “plant based”. Through reports like these, they manufacture new knowledge and consensus in creating systems that brings them more profits under the garb of science.

The Meat of the Matter provides a scientific understanding of major food and public health nutrition related controversies in India. Karpagam challenges the narrative of the vegetarian discourse of nutrition by juxtaposing it with majoritarianism. While she does not mention her methodology, or how she has collected her data, or selected her themes, this book can be read as a synthesis of the several structural harms that have been triggered by food and food cultures. I felt a deeper reading of the history of caste and violence in food politics and a critical perspective on policies that have led to our current nutritional systems could have been included. For instance, why do certain nutrients and foods become ‘heroes’ in certain decades or junctures. These include the rise of protein in the 1950s to the 70s, the micronutrients turn in the 90s, and later the emergence of ‘smarter foods’ like bio-fortification and fortification by nutrients. These events have shaped nutrition policies globally.

Although she mentions and acknowledges situated traditional knowledge of community in nourishment practices, we do not find in Karpagam's narrative a reference to the debates over how a biomedical approach to malnutrition can be a problematic hegemony, especially for countries in the Global South, where land dispossession, colonisation, caste location and socio economic factors shape nutrition. Yet, the accessible language used to present the science makes The Meat of the Matter an important book for people to understand food and nutrition politics in India.

Sayan Deori is a PhD scholar at Tezpur University, Assam. 

Independent Source: The India Forum

item.title: India permits E100 ethanol fuel for compatible flex-fuel vehicles
item.description:
🇮🇳 Indian Economy • The Hindu BusinessLine

The government has allowed the use of E100 ethanol fuel in vehicles specifically designed to run on flexible fuel, under amendments to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, notified by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.

According to the Gazette notification, the government has included E100 alongside E85 in the emission standards prescribed for flex-fuel vehicles, paving the way for vehicles designed to operate on nearly pure ethanol.

The notification, issued under G.S.R. 911(E), states, “E85 or E100 shall be used in the vehicles designed by the original equipment manufacturers as Flex-fuel vehicles.”

E100 refers to fuel containing 100 per cent ethanol, while E85 contains 85 per cent ethanol. Flex-fuel vehicles are designed to operate on different blends of petrol and ethanol.

Use restricted to vehicles designed for ethanol blends

The amendment is significant as India seeks to expand the use of ethanol in transport and reduce its dependence on conventional petrol. However, the provision applies specifically to vehicles designed by manufacturers for such fuels and does not permit their use in all petrol-powered vehicles.

Under the amended rules, references to “E85” in multiple provisions of Rule 115, which deals with vehicle emission standards, have been replaced with “E85 or E100”.

Gross vehicle weight threshold revised

The government has also revised the gross vehicle weight threshold specified in the relevant emission standards from 3,000 kg to 3,500 kg.

The notification states that “the figure and words ‘3500 kg’ shall be substituted” in place of the earlier 3,000 kg limit.

Amendments follow public consultation

The amendments follow draft rules issued on April 27, 2026, inviting objections and suggestions from stakeholders.

The ministry said that “the objections and suggestions received from the public in respect of the said draft rules have been considered by the Central Government.”

According to the notification, the amended rules will come into force from the date of their publication in the Official Gazette.

The changes provide a regulatory framework for E100-compatible flex-fuel vehicles, although the notification does not announce any timeline for the commercial availability of E100 fuel across the country.

Published on October 26, 2026

Source: The Hindu BusinessLine

item.title: Meta announces $95bn fundraising drive to pay for AI expansion – business live
item.description:
🌍 Major Global Event • The Guardian Economics
From 36m ago
07.41 EDT

Meta to raise $95bn to help fund AI plans

Boom! Meta has just announced plans to raise up to $95bn to help pay for its massive AI ambitions.

The company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp is kicking off a new fundraising drive to fund “its core business and emerging AI opportunities”.

The fundraising comes in two parts.

First, Meta plans to raise $35bn through new “underwritten public offerings” – a sale of company stock.

This offering has some big name backers – Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have all shown interest in taking part, Meta says. These ‘cornerstone investors’ could buy up to $5bn of the stock on offer.

Second, Meta also plans to launch a $60bn “at-the-market offering” – in which it will sell new common stock to investors at the going market rate in future.

The Silicon Valley giant says these plans will support “Meta’s continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”.

It also says it is “investing with financial discipline,” saying:

AI is creating significant opportunities for Meta across its core business and new products and services. Meta’s AI investments are already generating tangible returns through increased engagement, improved advertising performance and increased monetization. Meta is also pursuing new opportunities across personal superintelligence, consumer and business agents, enterprise products, and AI glasses.

The ‘at the market offering’ involves selling Meta’s new Class C Stock, which it announced last week it is creating. These Class C shares don’t have voting rights, so can be sold without diluting founder Mark Zuckerberg’s control of the company.

Internal forecasts last week showed that Meta needs to raise “hundreds of billions of dollars” over several years to fund its AI plans.

1h ago07.09 EDT

The downturn in UK retail sales has eased this month, new data shows.

The CBI reports that UK retail sales volumes contracted in the year to October at the slowest rate since April 2025.

A net balance of -10% retailers reported that sales dropped over the last year, better than the -55% recorded in September.

Martin Sartorius, lead economist at the CBI, says:

“The ongoing retail sales downturn eased in October, with volumes falling at their slowest annual pace in over a year. Wholesalers and motor traders also saw some signs of activity steadying over the same period. That said, the outlook remains fragile as businesses face headwinds from cautious household spending and higher fuel costs.

Share
2h ago06.14 EDT

UK gilt yields dropping ahead of the budget

UK government borrowing costs are dropping this morning, a welcome sign ahead of Wednesday’s budget.

The yield (or interest rate) on 10 and 30-year UK gilts have both dropped by around three basis points (0.03 of a percentage point) this morning.

City investors are hoping that chancellor John Healey avoids rocking the boat when he delivers his first budget, prioritising rebuilding fiscal headroom – although the jump in bond yields in recent months will have eaten into that borrowing cushion.

There were reports last weekend that Healey will put billions of pounds into public financial institutions including the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank.

Fresh funding into these so-called “PuFins” could boost the UK’s AI, defence and green energy sectors.

Crucially for the chancellor, if a PuFin makes a loan or investment, the value of this financial asset is netted off against public liabilities, and the PSNFL measure of UK debt does not go up.

However, the City may be wary of any trickery to keep government debt off the books.

Andrew Wishart, UK economist at Berenberg, explains:

Issuing loans to public financial institutions creates a financial asset that offsets the increase in outstanding government debt. If the investments that the PuFins make generate sufficient returns for the PuFins to repay their government loans, then long term debt sustainability is little affected.

Limited transparency and the risk that the PuFins may suffer impairments on their investments will probably make bond market investors skeptical of the extra gilt issuance. Chancellor Healey should avoid a big increase in gilt issuance to fund such intra-public sector lending.

Neocloud company shares drop after Musk warning

Shares in AI cloud computing companies are dropping in pre-market trading after Elon Musk warned they face “guppy-level death and consolidation”.

Coreweave are down 2.4% in pre-market. Nebius, another neocloud operator, are on track for a 2.1% drop when Wall Street opens, while Iren are down 1.9%.

Neil Wilson, Saxo UK investor strategist, says:

Nebius, CoreWeave and Iren were slammed in premarket trading on Monday after SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said more than 200 neoclouds are “going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.”

That’s the guppy fish – prone to suddenly dying in household fisk tanks – not the GBPJPY FX cross...In a post on X Musk said “debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers”.

Share
3h ago05.44 EDT

Business sentiment in Germany has improved, as hopes build that its economic stagnation may be ending.

Economic research institute Ifo’s Business Climate Index has risen to 90.2 points in October, up from 89.9 points in September.

Ifo reports:

This was due to more optimistic expectations. Companies, however, assessed their current situation as slightly worse. The economic recovery is continuing.

Share
3h ago05.28 EDT

Brazil's bonds fall after Lula wins election

Elsewhere in the bond markets, Brazil’s debt is dropping in value after president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a dramatic victory over his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.

Bolsonaro, son of the former president, had been expected to oust Lula, but instead the left-wing incumbent triumphed, with 51.79% of the vote to his 45-year-old rival’s 48.21%.

Investors had anticipated that a Bolsonaro win would have led to a new push to rein in Brazil’s public debt, and may now be keen to sell Brazilian debt and the real.

Reuters reports that Brazil’s international bonds have dropped more than 1 cent after Lula’s election win.

Viktor Szabó, investment director for emerging market debt at Aberdeen Investments, explains why bond investors are nervous:

Lula’s campaign did pledge fiscal consolidation, but at a slower pace than his rival and with the explicit condition that spending cuts should not fall on lower-income Brazilians. The government’s own projections show the primary balance improving only gradually, to a surplus of 1.3% of GDP by 2030. His running mate, Geraldo Alckmin, pointed to campaign funding and excessive public-sector salaries as areas for savings. Neither comes close to the scale of the problem.

Brazil has little room left for this kind of politics. Gross public debt has climbed to around 83% of GDP, up more than 10 percentage points during this administration, and a deficit close to 10% of GDP is now almost entirely interest. Brazil pays one of the highest real interest rates in the world on a debt that keeps growing, which is the definition of an unsustainable path, and the bill falls on companies and households as much as on the Treasury.

Share
Updated at 05.36 EDT
3h ago04.49 EDT

Elon Musk’s warning that AI cloud funding could dry up is a reminder that companies may not provide the revenues that hyperscalers and neoclouds are relying on.

Steve Daheb, Head of AI GTM Strategy at enterprise software firm Flexera, explains:

“We have spent the past few years debating whether AI will replace people. But the more immediate question for many businesses is whether AI could end up costing more than the people and processes it replaces.

“Businesses need to remember every decision an AI makes and every action an agent takes has a price tag. The AI people see and the prompt they enter is only part of the story. AI doesn’t just answer questions: it reasons, retries, checks and refines its response, drawing on models, enterprises data and computing power just to complete a single task. That iterative process and response refinement are what drive AI costs. Once agents are embedded across applications and running tasks throughout a business, the metre is always running – yet many companies still have no idea how many tokens they are using or what a particular task will cost because of this AI cost domino effect.

“That is why we are seeing such whiplash. Businesses went from board-level mandates to use AI as quickly as possible to cancelling licences, imposing token limits and slamming the brakes on projects when the bills arrived.”

Share
4h ago04.38 EDT

French bonds rally after Paris avoids Moody's downgrade

French government bonds are rallying this morning after Paris avoided being downgrade by rating agency Moody’s last Friday night.

The yield, or interest rate, on French 10-year bonds has dropped by 3.5 basis points to 4.98%, away from the 24-year high set last week.

Moody’s surprised investors late on Friday night by announcing it had maintained its rating of Aa3 with a negative outlook; the City had expected a cut.

Moody’s warned, though, that France’s debt position has worsened, explaining:

Since our previous periodic review of the sovereign rating, slower growth and a higher deficit have pushed France’s debt burden somewhat higher than previously expected. In addition, government bond yields have risen more rapidly than we expected, while widespread social protests have erupted which could constrain fiscal consolidation efforts.

The Aa3 rating assumes that a deficit-reducing budget for 2027 will be adopted, while financing costs and social tensions will abate somewhat in the next few months.

France’s public debt soared to 119% of GDP this summer, the highest level since 1946. The proposed budget for 2027, which has yet to be approved, aims to cut France’s budget deficit from 5.4% to 5% through wage freezes and tax rises.

Share
4h ago04.15 EDT

UK's Computacenter hikes profit forecasts thanks to AI demand

UK tech company Computacenter is benefitting from the AI boom.

This morning, Computacenter raised its financial outlook for this financial year, after “a very strong first half performance”.

Computercenter is winning business from the neoclouds – the AI cloud computing companies which Elon Musk reckons face ‘guppy-level death’.

It told the City:

Sourcing revenue continued to grow strongly, primarily driven by hyperscale and neocloud customers in North America and the UK.

Group Services revenue was also ahead of last year, as strong organic growth in Professional Services, also driven by North America, more than offset a decline in Managed Services revenue.

There’s such demand that Computercenter now has a ‘committed product order backlog’ of £12.6bn, up from £9.3bn at the end of June, and “a strong pipeline of opportunities in North America and the UK”.

It now expects adjusted profit before tax for FY 2026 to be at least £425m, ahead of forecasts of £387.1m.

Shares have jumped by 6.7% in early trading.

They’ve heard that talks over the pricing of this deal are still ongoing, and report:

As of late Sunday in New York, those conversations remained ongoing and the deal hadn’t priced, people with knowledge of the discussions said. The parties are still working on finalizing the debt package in the coming days, the people said.

Introduction: Musk says AI datacentre funding is drying up

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

The flow of funding which has helped the AI industry to grow rapidly could be running dry, at least for some firms in the cloud computing world, Elon Musk has warned.

The world’s richest person declared last night that at least 200 ‘neoclouds’ – companies which provide specialised cloud infrastructure to run AI workloads – could die or consolidate because they will struggle to access capital.

Musk made the claim while also declaring that his SpaceX business has closed a $40bn debt deal to pay for the chips it needs for its artificial intelligence work.

He posted on X that firms who rely on revenue streams from AI datacentres are being cold-shouldered by lenders, saying:

As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers.

SpaceX closed $40B of debt for GPUs, but we’re investment grade and have Starlink & launch revenue.

That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many.

[Musk is referring to the guppy fish, the colourful freshwater aquarium fish notorious for suddenly dying in the aquarium, especially if there is a change in its environment.]

Neoclouds are specialist cloud providers that rent out clusters of high-speed Nvidia chips to firms looking to conduct AI training and inference.

They include CoreWeave, the US firm whose share price has fallen 60% in the last year as investors have questioned whether the huge investment in AI datacentres will be rewarded with lucrative cash flows.

The cost of insuring CoreWeave’s debt against default has climbed in recent weeks to levels that typically suggest credit distress – Musk’s comments are unlikely ease investors concerns!

item.title: Wall Street's fastest traders are building data centers and backing chip startups to stay ahead in AI
item.description:
🤖 AI & Tech • The Decoder
Short News
Copy the url to clipboard Share this article Go to comment section
Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner
Oct 26, 2026

High-frequency traders like Jane Street and Hudson River Trading are now racing each other for AI computing power. The biggest firms are spending billions on cloud contracts, startups, and their own data centers, Bloomberg reports. Part of the reason is that they increasingly rely on machine learning to predict market moves.

One executive estimates that compute spending is now ten to twenty times higher than it was before ChatGPT launched. XTX Markets is building a data center in Finland, and Jane Street runs one in Texas with more than 4,000 Nvidia GPUs. Hudson River spends $1 billion a year on AI, according to AI chief Iain Dunning, and signed a multiyear deal with CoreWeave. Jane Street went a different route. It invested $1 billion directly in CoreWeave and committed $6 billion to its computing services.

Jane Street also led a funding round for chip startup Etched and became the first customer for its AI chip, which is supposed to deliver more performance by running at a lower voltage. According to Bloomberg, the industry sees rising costs and fast-aging chips as real risks. Executives like Jan Boomaars, CEO of Amsterdam-based high-frequency trader Optiver, still think doing nothing is more dangerous.
